In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to HIV-1 therapy, based on gene therapy with plas-mids encoding IFN-I.
the development of gene therapy approaches that can prevent the depletion of CD4 T cells and control viral replication in HIV-1 infection.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for HIV/AIDS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IFN-β is the most potent antiviral agent against HIV-1 and that IFN-α subtypes have different antiviral effects.
the Hu-PBL humanized mouse model, which is characterized by the absence of IFN-1, is a suitable model for testing gene therapy approaches against HIV-1 infection.
IFN-β is superior to IFN-α2 and IFN-β/IFN-α14 in the prevention of HIV-1-induced CD4 T cell destruction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IFN-β has a superior antiviral activity against HIV-1 in the Hu-PBLC mouse model, compared to IFN-α subtypes.
the Hu-PBL humanized mouse model is an ideal model for testing the effect of IFN-I in the context of HIV infection.
IFN-β has the best therapeutic potential for HIV-1 infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gene therapy with IFN-β is a promising strategy to treat HIV-1.
IFN-β is superior to IFN-α2 in preventing CD4 T cell loss and reducing viral load in the humanized mouse model.
the choice of IFN-I subtype is important for the development of gene therapy strategies for HIV-1 infection.
